chapters.title: Chapter 6: Putting Alternatives Into Your Portfolio

lessons.title: Case Study: A Bengaluru Professional With 50 Lakh Rupees vs a Mumbai HNI With 10 Crore Rupees

children.text: Two investors receive almost the same WhatsApp forwards and relationship manager pitches: a fractional office in Whitefield, an SM REIT, a pre-IPO deal, an angel platform, a P2P app, a PE fund. One is a 31-year-old product designer in Bengaluru with ₹50 lakh. The other is a Mumbai family with ₹10 crore and a rented flat in Powai. This lesson runs both through every tool in the course: real returns, the four risks, the scorecard and the sizing steps. The same pitches get very different answers, and in both cases the most important decision turns out to be about something they already own.

body.text: The right amount of alternatives is decided by your balance sheet, not by the opportunity. For most investors with modest wealth, the answer is almost none. For wealthy investors, the answer often starts with fixing an alternative they already hold.

columns.label: Priyanka Nair, 31, Bengaluru
points: Product designer at a fintech startup, monthly expenses about ₹1 lakh
₹50 lakh total: ₹22 lakh equity mutual funds, ₹10 lakh savings, ₹8 lakh FDs, ₹6 lakh unlisted ESOPs, ₹4 lakh gold jewellery
Goal: ₹25 lakh down payment for a flat in about 4 years
Rents her home; no property, no debt
Pitched: a fractional office, an SM REIT, angel investing, a P2P app, pre-IPO shares and crypto

columns.label: Rajesh and Nisha Shah, 48 and 46, Mumbai
points: Rajesh is a senior banker, Nisha runs a small design studio; monthly expenses about ₹2.5 lakh
₹10 crore in liquid financial investments, plus a rented Powai flat worth about ₹3 crore, bought in 2012 for ₹1.2 crore
Goals: children's overseas education, about ₹1.5 crore over the next 8 years; retirement in about 12 years
Own the home they live in, no loans
Pitched: a PE AIF, a private credit AIF, a real estate AIF, a Category III long-short fund, pre-IPO shares and a second flat

children.text: Priyanka passes most gates: no debt, a job with a steady salary, and more than enough cash for a six-month emergency fund of ₹6 lakh. But her flat down payment of ₹25 lakh is due in about four years, well inside any alternative's lock-in. That money must sit in liquid, lower-risk assets, not in equity and certainly not in anything illiquid.

cells: Up to 5% for ₹25 lakh to ₹1 crore of wealth

children.text: Her ESOPs alone are more than twice her illiquid cap, and they are startup risk in the same ecosystem that pays her salary. Her jewellery is another 8% in gold. Priyanka already holds about 20% of her wealth in alternative-type assets without having bought a single product.

data.label: Down payment fund (short-term debt and FDs)

body.text: The biggest improvement to Priyanka's portfolio has nothing to do with alternatives. Moving most of her ₹22 lakh equity funds towards a safer down payment fund protects her main goal from a crash just before she buys. She should check the capital gains tax on switching and plan any sale around it. Her best "alternative strategy" is to say no to every illiquid pitch for now and sell some ESOPs when she is allowed to.

children.text: Step 1: The flat they forgot to count

The Shahs think of themselves as having ₹10 crore to invest. But the Powai flat is an investment too: ₹3 crore of illiquid, concentrated, appraisal-priced real estate. At a typical Mumbai gross yield of about 2.5%, it pays roughly ₹7.5 lakh a year before costs and tax, which Chapter 4 showed can leave a real return close to zero. Their true investable wealth is ₹13 crore, and 23% of it is already in one illiquid alternative.

body.title: How much room is left?
body.prompt: The Shahs' investable wealth, including the Powai flat, is ₹13 crore. Suppose they cap illiquid alternatives at 25% of investable wealth. The flat is worth ₹3 crore. How much room is left for new illiquid alternatives, in crore?
body.explanation: 25% × ₹13 crore = ₹3.25 crore. Minus the ₹3 crore flat leaves ₹0.25 crore, or ₹25 lakh. Every AIF pitched to them needs ₹1 crore, so while they keep the flat, none of them fit.

body.title: Keep the flat or sell it

columns.label: Path A: keep the Powai flat
points: Illiquid room for new alternatives: about ₹25 lakh
No AIF fits; at most a small SM REIT or a few angel cheques
Portfolio stays 23% in one Mumbai property
Rental income continues, with low real return and tenant effort

points: Frees about ₹2.8 crore after brokerage and tax
Illiquid cap rises to about ₹3.2 crore, with a single-position cap near ₹1.3 crore
Room for a diversified, paced set of fund commitments
Replaces one concentrated asset with several diversified ones

children.text: The ₹2 crore for illiquid alternatives is about 16% of investable wealth, below the ₹3.2 crore cap, leaving room for mistakes and for the denominator effect in a crash. It is committed in stages: the PE fund first, a second manager or strategy a year or two later. Until capital is called, the committed money sits in a liquid fund. The listed REITs and gold ETFs add diversification without using the illiquid budget.

body.title: The common thread
body.question: What single step changed the answer most in both case studies?
options: Picking the alternative with the highest expected return
Counting the alternative-type assets each investor already owned before sizing new ones
Waiting for a stock market crash before investing
Choosing products with the lowest minimum ticket
body.explanation: Priyanka's ESOPs already exceeded her illiquid cap, and the Shahs' flat used up almost all of theirs. Once existing holdings were counted, the right amount of new alternatives changed completely in both cases.

body.title: Indexation
body.textWithBlank: The number used to adjust a property's purchase cost for inflation when calculating indexed capital gains is called the Cost ___ Index.
body.explanation: The Cost Inflation Index is notified each year. For property bought before 23 July 2024, individuals can still choose 20% tax with indexation instead of 12.5% without it, whichever results in less tax.

body.title: Now it is your turn: Dr Farah Khan
body.scenario: Dr Farah Khan, 44, a dermatologist in Hyderabad, has ₹2 crore of investable wealth: ₹1.1 crore in equity mutual funds, ₹50 lakh in FDs and debt funds, ₹25 lakh in gold ETFs and SGBs, and ₹15 lakh in savings. She owns the home she lives in, has no other property or business stake, and her monthly expenses are about ₹2 lakh. Her daughter's medical college fees of about ₹40 lakh fall due in 3 years. She is pitched a ₹10 lakh SM REIT holding one pre-leased warehouse, and an angel platform suggesting ₹10 lakh across two startups.
body.prompt: Run Dr Khan through the sizing steps and evaluate both pitches.
body.modelAnswer:
Sizing:
- Investable wealth: ₹2 crore.
- Emergency fund: 6 to 12 months of expenses, say ₹24 lakh at 12 months.
- Goal within the lock-in: ₹40 lakh of college fees in 3 years.
- Lockable capital: ₹200 − ₹24 − ₹40 = ₹136 lakh.
- Illiquid cap for ₹1 to 5 crore of wealth: 5 to 15%, say 10% = ₹20 lakh.
- Single-position cap: about 5% = ₹10 lakh.
- Existing illiquid alternatives: none (gold ETFs and SGBs are tradeable, and her home is excluded).
- Room for new illiquid alternatives: about ₹20 lakh, with no single position above ₹10 lakh.

SM REIT, ₹10 lakh: fits the single-position cap exactly, so it is possible. But on the Chapter 5 scorecard, a single-warehouse, single-tenant SM REIT scores poorly on downside and liquidity. She should compare its after-tax yield with a listed REIT and consider a smaller or no allocation.

Angel investing, ₹10 lakh across two startups: two bets give poor odds under the power law, and ₹5 lakh per startup at most could not be repeated enough to build a real portfolio within her ₹20 lakh cap. A better route, if she wants startup exposure, is many small cheques over several years or skipping it.

Before either: move the ₹40 lakh college fund into low-risk, liquid assets if it is currently in equity funds. That protects the one goal that cannot move.

points: The same pitches get opposite answers for different balance sheets, so the investor, not the product, decides the allocation.
Priyanka's unlisted ESOPs already exceeded her illiquid cap, so the right amount of new illiquid alternatives was zero, and protecting her down payment mattered most.
The Shahs' ₹3 crore Powai flat used up almost their entire illiquid budget, leaving just ₹25 lakh of room while they kept it.
Selling the flat, with indexation saving about ₹8 lakh in tax, would free about ₹2.8 crore and make a paced, diversified set of fund commitments possible.
Even for the Shahs, alternatives stay a satellite of about 16% around a core of listed equity, fixed income and gold.
Always count existing property, business stakes, ESOPs and jewellery before sizing any new alternative.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or tax advice. The investors, products and figures are hypothetical and illustrative. Allocation caps are general guidance, not rules. Tax calculations are simplified and exclude surcharge and exemptions. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser and a qualified tax professional before making decisions.
